full_judgment:
4. It appears that on 9-4-60 the appellants filed an application in the Court for particulars of non-impleaded contiguous owners where upon the Court directed the contesting opposite party to furnish the said particulars on 21.4.60 the contesting opposite party furnished the names of 8 persons who were, according to her, the contiguous owners who were not are parties in the said proceeding. An application was. thereupon filed by the appellants on 4-6-60 in which it was contended that the said persons were not the holders of contiguous lands as their interests had already been transferred by their predecessor to Opposite Party No. 66 and that, in view of the objection, however, they might be Impleaded as parties; and thereafter the said 8 persons were impleaded as proforma Opposite-parties No. 89 to 96. 

 11. The question of joinder of parties is essentially a matter of procedure and some detailed rules have been provided in the Code of Civil Procedure on the question of joinder of parties. Order 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure deals with the question of the parties to a suit and by virtue of section 141 the Code the said provisions are applicable to a proceeding of original nature like the one under section 96 of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. It has, however, been laid down in Order 1, rule 9 that no suit shall be defeated by reason of the mis-joinder or non-joinder of parties, and the court may in every suit deal with the matter in controversy so far as regards the rights and interests of the parties actually before it and rule 13 of the said Order provides that all objections on the ground of non-joinder and mis-joinder of parties shall be taken at the earliest possible opportunity and any such objection not so taken shall be deemed to have been waived. Under the rules of pleading also, any objection as to the maintainability of a suit which requires investigation of facts, must be taken in the pleading before the framing of the issues so that the other party may not be taken by surprise and be prejudiced in respect of the defence which may have been taken by him to meet the said objection. Order 8, rule 2 of the Code Jays down, inter alia, that the defendant must raise by his pleading all matters which show the suit not to be maintainable and all such grounds of defence as, if not raised, would be likely to take the opposite party by surprise or would raise issues of fact not arising out of the plaint. When the objection is to be taken to the effect that the suit or proceeding is incompetent because of the absence of a necessary party such an objection necessarily involves questions of fact and is controlled also by the rule of pleading as embodied in the aforesaid Order 8, rule 2 Civil Procedure Code. 

 12. As we have already noticed, an objection on the question of defect of parties was taken in the petition of objection and certain names were mentioned therein who, according to the pre-emptee opposite party, were owners of contiguous lands and as such where necessary parties. But when the pre-emptors petitioners filed an application for particulars of the said persons and the Trial Court directed the pre-emptee opposite party to furnish the particulars of the non-impleaded persons, the pre-emptee opposite party furnished a list of 8 persons who, according to her, were the necessary parties for the purpose of said proceeding. Although the said names were different from those which were mentioned in her petition of objection, the said person were, however, impleaded in the preemption proceeding as proforma opposite parties and no objection as to the defect of parties was pressed at the time of hearing of the case. Only a question as to the delay in impleading the said proforma opposite parties was agitated in the appellate court of the Subordinate Judge. The objection as to defect of party appears to have been clearly governed by the provision of Order 1, rule 11 of the Code, according to which the said objection is deemed to have been waived. This objection, as it involves ascertainment of certain facts, comes in conflict also with the rule of pleading as provided in Order 8, rule 2 C.P. Code. In the circumstances prima facie, the pre-emptee purchaser ought not to have been allowed to urge this objection for the first time in the Revisional Court. 

 15. The view which has been expressed in the aforesaid decision to the effect that Order 1, rule 9 of the Code does not apply if the cause of action arises against a number of persons jointly and that in the case of pre-emption under section 96 of the Act the cause of action arises not only against the transferee but also against the co-sharers and other holders of contiguous lands requires careful consideration. It is difficult to place a suit for partition and a case for pre-emption on the same footing on the question of joinder of parties. In a suit for partition the co-sharers are necessary parties in the sense that in the absence of any such co-sharer the judgment which will be given in such a suit may be rendered infructuous at the option of the excluded party. It is correct to say that in such a suit the cause of action for partition arises in favour of the co-sharers suing for partition as against all the remaining co-sharers because every one of them has a substantive interest in every bit of the property which is the subject matter of the said suit. In order to give relief in such a suit, the Court shall have to determine the right, title and interest of the plaintiff-co-sharers specifically and as also right, title and interest of the defendant co-sharers specifically or impliedly, whether or not such co-sharer defendants apply for sahams. The question of parties in such a suit is considered entirely on a different footing, not because the provisions of Order 1, rule 9 or Order 1, rule 13 are not applicable to such a suit but because the trial of such a suit is subject to another principles which is to the effect that no Court shall pass a decree which may be set at nought at the instance of a person who is not impleaded in the said suit. It does not however mean that a suit for partition is beyond the pale of the procedural rules, such as Order 1, rule 13 and Order 8, rule 2 C.P. Code. Such rules are very much applicable in a suit for partition in the same way as in other classes of suits, and a party is precluded from taking at a late stage an objection as defect of party of which sufficient notice has not been given to the other side, even in a suit for partition. But the trial of a suit or proceeding is subject to the well recognised principle, which is calculated to advance the cause of justice, namely, that no court should pass a decree or make an order which is infructuous. A decree in a suit for partition in the absence of a co-sharer can be rendered valueless and infructuous at the option of the excluded co-Sharer, and if from the materials on record it appears to the Court that such a necessary party has been excluded in the suit, the Court shall, notwithstanding the absence of necessary pleading, stay its hand from passing the decree. 

 16. A proceeding for pre-emption, in our opinion, cannot be treated on the same level as a suit for partition. It is not correct to say that when a particular piece of land or share thereof is transferred, a right of pre-emption arises against all the co-sharers or contiguous owners, as the case may be. It may have accrued in favour of all the co-sharers of the seller of the land or the owners of the contiguous land, as the case may be, but it arises only against the purchaser. Ordinarily, there is no question of improper constitution of a pre-emption proceeding on account of the absence of the non-pre-empting co-sharers or contiguous owners. In a proceeding for pre-emption under section 26F of the Bengal Tenancy Act or section 24 of the East Bengal Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act, under which only the co-sharers have the right of pre-emption, it is not necessary to join all the co-sharers in such a proceeding for pre-emption. There is nothing inherently defective in the constitution of such a proceeding in the absence of the remaining co-sharers but the Legislature, in order to avoid multiplicity of the litigation, has provided in sub-section (2) of the section 96, that in addition to the transferee, the co-sharer tenants of the holding as well as the holders of the contiguous lands shall be made parties and sub-section (4) of the said section provided that such co-sharer tenants or holders of contiguous lands shall have to apply within the period referred to in sub-section (1) i.e., 4 months from the date of knowledge, or within 2 months of the date of the service of the notice of the application, whichever is earlier, and such of the persons as have not applied either under sub-section (1) or under the said sub-section shall not have any further right to purchase under section 96. This provision appears to have been enacted by the Legislature for the benefit of the persons seeking for pre-emption so that they may not be harassed by multiplicity of litigations in future. It does not appear from a perusal of the provisions of section 96 that it was the intent of the Legislature that the penalty for non-impleading a person as contemplated in sub-section (2) is the invalidity of the order which may be ultimately made in the said proceeding. The question whether a person is a necessary party under sub-section (2) is a question of fact and the object of this provision seems to provide the co-sharer tenants and the holders of the contiguous lands with the opportunity of availing themselves of the provision of the said sub-section. Since the benefit conferred under the said provision is meant for certain individuals, they can very well be waived. In that view of the matter the positive injunction contained in the said sub-section as to the making of parties inspite of its being couched in mandatory language, should be read as directory. 

 20. The learned Single Judge of the Dacca High Court relied upon the said principle in holding in the instant case that the pre-emption proceeding would not be affected for non-substitution of the heirs of several deceased opposite parties who died during the pendency of the revisional. proceeding in the High Court, as the right of the said opposite parties to pre-empt had already been barred under sub-section (1) of Section 96, but the learned Judge did not examine the question of non-joinder of Muzaffar Ali Khan in the light of the said principle. 

 21. Now even if the view that the pre-emption proceeding may be held to be non-maintainable in the absence of any of the necessary parties, i.e., any of the co-sharers or contiguous owners, as the case may be, is correct, the question whether Muzaffar Ali Khan was a necessary party in the pre-emption proceeding as alleged by the respondent involves ascertainment of two kinds of fact. The Court is to determine not only that the non-impleaded person was an owner of the contiguous lands on the date of the application filed by the appellants, but also that his right of pre-emption was not barred at the date when such application was filed. 

 28. In this connection section 99 of the Code of Civil Procedure may also be noticed. According to the said provision no decree shall be reversed or substantially varied nor shall any care be remanded in appeal on account of mis-joinder of parties or causes of action or any error, defect or irregularity in any proceeding of the suit not affecting the merits of the case or the jurisdiction of the Court. The principle underlying the said provision is of general application and is not to be confined to suits only but is, in our opinion, applicable to the present proceedings also. The Judicial Committee of the Privy Council has applied the said principle to a proceeding before the said Committee to which the Civil Procedure Code is not applicable on the view that "the rule embodied in section 99 provides sound principle and is calculated to promote justice" in the case of Mohammad Hossain Khan and others Vs. Babu Kishva Nandan Shansi L.R. 64 I.A. page 250 (same case) A.I.R. 1937 P.C. 233 (same case) 41 C.W.N. 1029.
